name: Allantoin
lead: Allantoin (5-ureidohydantoin) is a mild, colourless skincare ingredient that brands add to moisturisers, lip balms, scar gels, shampoos and sun care to leave skin feeling smoother, softer and less irritated. For appearance, the payoff people look for is a hydrated, calmer-looking complexion and, in scar and wound products, support for skin that is recovering from damage.[1][9]

Chemically it is a nitrogen-containing ureide produced when uric acid is oxidised. Most mammals make it enzymatically; humans do not, and form only small amounts through reactions with reactive oxygen species. It also occurs in plants such as comfrey, and cosmetic-grade allantoin is generally made synthetically and described as chemically equivalent to the natural form.[1]

Clinical research on allantoin is mostly on combination products, particularly scar and wound formulations, so its individual contribution is hard to isolate. No registered trial tests allantoin alone for facial appearance, but the studies that exist cover scars after caesarean section, intertrigo, cold sores and rare blistering skin disease.[3][4][5][6][7][8]

paras: Cosmetic descriptions credit allantoin with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and moisturising actions, and as a humectant that offsets drying ingredients such as alcohols, sulfates and fragrances.[1] It turns up in lotions, toothpaste, mouthwash, shampoos, lipsticks, anti-acne products and sun care.[1][9]

In cosmetic formulas allantoin is typically listed as a skin-conditioning agent at low concentrations, with a published range of roughly 0.0001 to 2 percent.[9] Brands position it as a soother for dry, rough or irritated skin and as a gentle partner to exfoliating or drying actives. Descriptions of its action include a keratolytic effect that loosens the dead surface layer so skin feels smoother, and support of the skin barrier, although these are described in secondary summaries rather than in trials of allantoin on its own.[9]

Allantoin is a recurring ingredient in scar gels and patches, usually alongside onion extract and heparin. A US over-the-counter label lists a topical product with 0.5 percent allantoin sold for scars, with directions to apply as needed and warnings to keep it out of the eyes and not to use it on deep or puncture wounds, animal bites or serious burns.[2] People who use these products are aiming for flatter, paler, less noticeable scars as skin remodels.

Allantoin is a colourless, odourless crystalline powder that dissolves moderately in water (about 0.57 g per 100 mL at 25 C).[1] It is chemically a diureide of glyoxylic acid and a derivative of hydantoin, and it is stable in mildly acidic to mildly alkaline formulas but breaks down in strong acids.[1][9]

In animals it arises from oxidation of uric acid during purine breakdown. In most mammals it is the main nitrogen waste in urine, while humans lack the enzyme and its presence in the body is used as a biomarker of oxidative stress.[1] Plant sources include comfrey root, and manufacturers also make it by oxidising uric acid or by condensing glyoxylic acid with urea.[1][9]

Cosmetic literature attributes three actions to allantoin: attracting and holding water at the skin surface as a humectant, mild anti-inflammatory and soothing activity, and a keratolytic effect that helps shed dull surface cells.[1][9] A 2010 laboratory report profiled the wound-healing process induced by allantoin, which is among the research behind claims that it promotes tissue repair.[10] The mechanisms are described mainly in secondary sources and animal or laboratory work, rather than in controlled trials of single-ingredient products.

Wikipedia describes the synthetic form as safe, non-toxic and compatible with cosmetic raw materials, citing a cosmetic ingredient safety assessment, and reports a rat oral LD50 above 5,000 mg per kg.[1] Grokipedia summarises safety assessments as finding it non-irritating and non-sensitising in reviewed cosmetic categories.[9] Product labels advise stopping use and consulting a doctor if the condition worsens or persists beyond seven days.[2]

Michele Buniva and Louis Vauquelin first isolated it in 1800, mistakenly believing it came from amniotic fluid; Jean Louis Lassaigne found it in allantoic fluid in 1821, and Wohler and Liebig synthesised it from uric acid in 1837.[1] Its name comes from the allantois, the fetal membrane in which it was first sought. A short note titled 'Allantoin' appeared in the British Medical Journal in 1967.[11]

Registered trials mostly use allantoin as one ingredient among several. They include a scar study of an onion-extract, allantoin and heparin product (120 participants),[3] an onion-extract and allantoin patch for caesarean scars (93 participants),[4] a Contractubex scar study after caesarean section (61 participants),[5] a trial of an allantoin-containing cream in intertrigo (40 participants) compared with hydrocortisone,[6] a cold-sore product study (80 participants),[7] and early trials in epidermolysis bullosa.[8] A published randomized trial of the intertrigo lotion compared a multi-ingredient adsorbent lotion containing allantoin with a low-potency corticosteroid.[12] Combination designs prevent attributing effects to allantoin alone.

Allantoin has also been a component in non-skin products, such as an alcohol-free antiseptic hand wash tested in 40 volunteers against an alcohol-based sanitiser.[14] Preclinical reports cited on Wikipedia describe improved insulin resistance in rats and extended lifespan in the worm C. elegans; these are not skin studies.[1]

card.summary: A classic soothing and moisturising additive in drugstore skincare; used in scar and wound combination products, rarely tested on its own.
card.note: Clinical studies are mostly on multi-ingredient products.

quick.overview:
Allantoin is a gentle, widely used skincare ingredient found in moisturisers, scar gels, lip products and sun care. Brands position it as soothing and hydrating.

Studies exist for scar and wound products that contain it, but they combine it with other ingredients, so its own effect is not isolated.
quick.mechanism: Cosmetic sources describe it as a humectant that attracts water and as having mild anti-inflammatory and antioxidant action. Humans do not make it enzymatically.
quick.risks: Described by Wikipedia as safe and non-toxic in cosmetic use, with a rat oral LD50 above 5,000 mg per kg.

chain: Applied in a cream, gel or balm at low concentration
Acts as a humectant and soothing agent that keeps the skin surface hydrated and comfortable
Smoother, less dry-looking skin and a supportive environment for healing scars
angle.text: Allantoin is used as a supporting ingredient: it holds moisture at the skin surface and is included in formulas meant to soothe irritation from stronger actives such as alcohols, sulfates or fragrances. In scar products it is paired with other ingredients, and people use these to improve how marks left by surgery or injury look as they mature.[1][9]
